categories.title: Queries
categories.blurb: Write statements that return the same correct rows at any table size and that an index can serve.

categories.title: Schema and data types
categories.blurb: Choose keys, types and constraints so that wrong data cannot be stored and the table does not need a rewrite later.

categories.title: Indexes
categories.blurb: Give each frequent query one index that fits it, and remove the indexes that only slow down writes.

categories.title: Transactions and concurrency
categories.blurb: Keep transactions short and make concurrent writers produce a correct result without blocking each other for long.

categories.title: Schema changes
categories.blurb: Change a live schema in steps that never hold a blocking lock for longer than a moment.

categories.title: Connections
categories.blurb: Keep the number of server processes small and give every client a pool, a role and time limits.

categories.title: Vacuum and bloat
categories.blurb: Let dead rows be removed as fast as they are produced, so tables stay compact and transaction IDs never run out.

categories.title: Observability and tuning
categories.blurb: Measure which statements cost the most before changing anything, and set the few parameters whose defaults do not fit a production server.

categories.title: Replication, high availability and backups
categories.blurb: Be able to restore the data to any moment and to lose a server without losing committed work.

categories.title: Security
categories.blurb: Give each role only the access it needs, encrypt and verify every connection, and keep secrets out of logs.

categories.title: Scaling
categories.blurb: Take the cheap steps first: tune one server, add replicas, partition and cache, and distribute data only at a measured limit.

rules.rule: End every paginated `ORDER BY` with a unique column
rules.why: Rows with equal sort values have no defined order among themselves, so they can swap places between two executions. A row then appears on two pages or on none. A unique last column, usually the primary key, makes the order total.
rules.avoid:
SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM articles
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;
rules.prefer:
SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM articles
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;

rules.rule: Page with a keyset condition instead of a growing `OFFSET`
rules.why: `OFFSET n` reads and discards n rows before it returns the first one, so `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40000` reads 40,020 rows. A keyset (seek) condition starts the index scan right after the last row of the previous page and reads only 20, at any depth. It also stays correct when rows are inserted between two requests.
rules.avoid:
SELECT id, created_at, total
FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40000;
rules.prefer:
-- $1, $2 = created_at and id of the last row on the previous page
SELECT id, created_at, total
FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- served by: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at DESC, id DESC);
rules.unless: A keyset cannot jump to an arbitrary page number; keep `OFFSET` for small result sets that need numbered pages.

rules.rule: List the columns in every `SELECT` and `INSERT` that application code sends
rules.why: `SELECT *` returns every column, including large ones stored out of line, prevents index-only scans, and changes shape when a column is added. An `INSERT` without a column list assigns values by position, so it fails or writes values into the wrong columns after a schema change.
rules.avoid:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = $1;

INSERT INTO customers VALUES (DEFAULT, $1, $2);

rules.rule: Give every `LIMIT` an `ORDER BY`
rules.why: Without `ORDER BY` the server returns rows in whatever order the chosen plan produces. The "first" rows change when the plan changes, after an update moves a row, or when a parallel scan is used, so the query returns an unpredictable subset.
rules.prefer:
SELECT id, status FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 1;
rules.unless: An existence check or a sample where any matching row is acceptable does not need an order.

rules.rule: Use `NOT EXISTS` instead of `NOT IN` with a subquery
rules.why: If the subquery returns a single NULL, `x NOT IN (…)` is never true and the query returns no rows, without an error. `NOT EXISTS` ignores NULLs and is planned as an anti join.

rules.rule: Compare the indexed column itself, not a function or cast of it
rules.why: A B-tree index on `created_at` stores `created_at` values. A predicate on `created_at::date` or `lower(email)` asks about a different value, so the planner cannot use that index and scans the whole table.

rules.rule: Filter timestamps with a half-open range: `>=` start and `<` end
rules.why: `BETWEEN` includes both ends. With an end of `2026-11-16` a row stamped exactly at midnight is counted in two consecutive days, and with an end of `23:59:59` the rows in the last second are lost. A half-open range puts every instant in exactly one period.
rules.avoid:
SELECT count(*) FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-11-15' AND '2026-11-16';

rules.rule: Test for existence with `EXISTS`, not with `count(*) > 0`
rules.why: `count(*)` reads every matching row before it compares the total with zero. `EXISTS` stops at the first match, which is one index probe when an index fits.
rules.avoid:
SELECT count(*) > 0 AS has_orders
FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1;

rules.rule: Do not run an exact `count(*)` over a large table on every request
rules.why: Each transaction sees its own set of rows, so there is no stored row count: `count(*)` has to visit every row or index entry and check its visibility. On a table of hundreds of millions of rows that is a full scan per page view.
rules.avoid:
-- total for a "1 of N pages" footer, run per request
SELECT count(*) FROM events;
rules.unless: Counts over a small, indexed subset are cheap; for exact totals shown often, maintain a counter table or a materialized view.

rules.rule: Pass values as bind parameters, never by concatenating them into the SQL text
rules.why: A value pasted into the statement is parsed as SQL, which is how SQL injection works. Parameters travel separately from the statement text, are never parsed as SQL, and let `pg_stat_statements` and prepared statements treat all executions as one query.
rules.avoid:
-- built in application code
"SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"

rules.rule: Fetch and write sets of rows in one statement instead of one statement per row
rules.why: A loop that runs one query per item (the N+1 pattern) pays a network round trip, a parse and a plan for each row; 1,000 items at 1 ms per round trip is a second of waiting. One statement with an array parameter or a join does the same work in one round trip.

rules.rule: Use `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` for surrogate primary keys
rules.why: An `integer` key ends at 2,147,483,647, and widening it later rewrites the table under an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock. `GENERATED ALWAYS` also rejects an explicit id (SQLSTATE `428C9`), so a stray insert cannot put the sequence out of step with the data.

rules.rule: When a key must be a UUID, store it as `uuid` and generate it with `uuidv7()`
rules.why: Random UUIDv4 keys land on random leaf pages of the primary-key index, so inserts dirty pages all over it and the index outgrows the cache. `uuidv7()`, built in since PostgreSQL 18, starts with a millisecond timestamp, so new keys append at the right edge like a sequence. The `uuid` type takes 16 bytes; the same value as `text` takes 37.
rules.unless: A UUIDv7 reveals its creation time; use `uuidv4()` for identifiers that must not leak it, and prefer `bigint` identity when ids are generated only by the database.

rules.rule: Store points in time as `timestamptz`, not `timestamp`
rules.why: `timestamp` (without time zone) silently drops any offset in the input and stores a wall-clock reading with no zone, so the same value means different instants to sessions in different zones. `timestamptz` stores an absolute instant in UTC and converts it to the session `TimeZone` on output. Both take 8 bytes.
rules.unless: A local wall-clock time that is not an instant, such as "shop opens at 09:00", belongs in `time` or `timestamp` next to a zone name.

rules.rule: Use `text` with a `CHECK` constraint instead of `varchar(n)` or `char(n)`
rules.why: `text`, `varchar(n)` and `char(n)` are stored the same way and perform the same; `char(n)` additionally pads values with spaces. A named `CHECK` states the real rule (length, format), gives a clear error, and can be tightened later with `NOT VALID` plus `VALIDATE` instead of a rewrite.

rules.rule: Store money and other exact decimals as `numeric`, never as `real` or `double precision`
rules.why: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions: `0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8` is 0.30000000000000004 and does not equal 0.3. Sums of such values drift by fractions of a cent. `numeric` computes exactly in decimal.
rules.unless: An integer count of the smallest unit (cents in `bigint`) is equally exact and faster to aggregate; floats are right for measurements.

rules.rule: Declare every column `NOT NULL` unless a missing value has a meaning
rules.why: NULL makes comparisons return unknown: `status <> 'paid'` skips NULL rows, `NOT IN` returns nothing, and aggregates ignore NULL inputs. A column that is nullable by accident forces every query to handle a case that should not exist.

rules.rule: Give every constraint an explicit name
rules.why: The constraint name is what an error reports and what a migration must reference to drop or validate it. A generated name is built from the table and column names and gets a number appended when it is already taken, so the same constraint can have different names in two databases and a migration written against one fails on the other.
rules.avoid: ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CHECK (balance >= 0);
rules.prefer:
ALTER TABLE accounts
  ADD CONSTRAINT accounts_balance_nonnegative CHECK (balance >= 0);
-- ERROR: new row for relation "accounts" violates
--        check constraint "accounts_balance_nonnegative"

rules.rule: Declare every reference between tables as a foreign key
rules.why: Without the constraint, a deleted parent or a mistyped id leaves rows that point at nothing, and no later query can tell which ones are wrong. Application-level checks cannot close the gap, because two concurrent transactions do not see each other before they commit.
rules.unless: A partition or shard layout that cannot express the reference needs a periodic consistency check instead.

rules.rule: Keep fields that you filter, join or constrain in typed columns; use `jsonb` only for attributes that really vary
rules.why: A key inside `jsonb` has no type, no `NOT NULL`, no foreign key and no planner statistics, so row estimates for filters on it are guesses. Changing one key rewrites the whole document, and every row repeats the key names.
rules.prefer:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku text NOT NULL,
  price numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,
  attrs jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',  -- per-category extras
  CONSTRAINT products_sku_key UNIQUE (sku)
);

rules.rule: Use an enum type only for a fixed set of values; use a lookup table when the set changes or carries data
rules.why: An enum value can be added or renamed but never removed, and a value added inside a transaction cannot be used until that transaction commits. A lookup table with a foreign key takes ordinary inserts and deletes and can hold attributes such as a label or a flag.
rules.avoid:
CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM ('new', 'paid', 'on_hold_q3_promo');
-- no ALTER TYPE ... DROP VALUE exists
rules.unless: An enum is 4 bytes and sorts in declaration order, which suits a small set that is stable for good, such as weekday names.

rules.rule: On very large tables, declare wide fixed-size columns before narrow ones
rules.why: Each value starts at a multiple of its type alignment, so a `boolean` followed by a `bigint` is followed by 7 padding bytes. The six columns below take 64 bytes per row when `boolean` columns alternate with wider ones and 47 when ordered 8-byte, 4-byte, 1-byte (row header included).
rules.unless: Below hundreds of millions of rows the saving is not worth a less readable column order, and columns added later go at the end anyway.

rules.rule: Prevent overlapping periods with an exclusion constraint, not with a check in the application
rules.why: Two sessions that each look for a conflicting booking and find none can both insert, because neither sees the other's uncommitted row. An exclusion constraint makes the server reject any row whose range overlaps (`&&`) an existing one for the same key, with SQLSTATE `23P01` (exclusion_violation), whatever the timing.
rules.prefer:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;   -- for "room_id WITH ="

CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id bigint NOT NULL,
  during tstzrange NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT bookings_no_overlap
    EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
rules.unless: Ranges are half-open by default, so a booking that ends at 11:00 does not conflict with one that starts at 11:00; the GiST index behind the constraint is slower to update than a B-tree.

rules.rule: Create an index on the referencing columns of every foreign key
rules.why: A foreign key indexes nothing on the referencing side. Each `DELETE` of a parent row, and each update of its key, must find the child rows, which is a sequential scan of the child table per parent row while holding locks. Joins from parent to child need the same index.
rules.avoid:
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders (id)
);  -- DELETE FROM orders scans all of order_items
rules.prefer: CREATE INDEX order_items_order_id_idx ON order_items (order_id);
rules.unless: A parent table whose rows are never deleted or re-keyed, and never joined to the child, does not need it.

rules.rule: Order composite index columns: equality columns first, then the range or sort column
rules.why: A B-tree is sorted by its first column, then the second within equal first values. With the equality columns first, all matching entries are one contiguous run that is already in the order of the next column, so the scan needs no sort and can stop at `LIMIT`.
rules.prefer:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);
rules.unless: PostgreSQL 18 can skip-scan an index whose leading column is not constrained, but it descends the tree once per distinct leading value, so it only helps when that column has few values.

rules.rule: Index only the rows and the expression that the query actually uses
rules.why: A partial index (one with a `WHERE` clause) over the few rows a query reads, such as unprocessed jobs, is smaller, stays in memory and is not touched by writes to other rows. An expression index stores the computed value, so a predicate on `lower(email)` can use it.
rules.avoid:
CREATE INDEX jobs_status_idx ON jobs (status);
-- 99% of the entries are 'done' rows that no query looks for
rules.unless: The query must repeat the index predicate or expression in a form the planner can match; a bind parameter in place of the constant `'queued'` can prevent that.

rules.rule: Add payload columns with `INCLUDE` for index-only scans, and keep the table vacuumed
rules.why: An index-only scan answers from the index alone, but only for heap pages marked all-visible in the visibility map, which `VACUUM` sets. On pages changed since the last vacuum it fetches every row from the table: `Heap Fetches` in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows how many.
rules.prefer:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_incl_idx
  ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total);
-- SELECT customer_id, total ... WHERE customer_id = $1
--   Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 0   (after VACUUM)
rules.unless: Every included column makes the index larger and stops HOT updates of that column, so include only small, rarely updated columns.

rules.rule: Build indexes on live tables with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and drop any index left `INVALID`
rules.why: A plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks every insert, update and delete on the table for the whole build. The concurrent form does not, but if it fails (deadlock, duplicate key, cancel) it leaves an `INVALID` index that queries ignore and every write still maintains.
rules.avoid: CREATE INDEX orders_status_idx ON orders (status);
rules.unless: It cannot run inside a transaction block, takes longer than a plain build, and waits for transactions that are older than itself; on a new or empty table use the plain form.

rules.rule: Remove indexes that no query uses and indexes that duplicate another
rules.why: Every index is written on each insert, on each update that is not HOT, and is vacuumed and kept in cache. An index with `idx_scan = 0` over a long period has only costs, and an index on `(a)` is redundant next to one on `(a, b)`.
rules.prefer:
SELECT s.relname, s.indexrelname, s.idx_scan,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0 AND NOT i.indisunique
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_idx;
rules.unless: Usage counters are kept per server and start at zero after a statistics reset: check every replica and a full business cycle before dropping, and keep indexes that enforce constraints.

rules.rule: Match the index type to the operator: GIN for containment and full text, GiST for ranges and geometry, BRIN for append-only time columns
rules.why: A B-tree serves equality, range comparisons (`<`, `>`, `BETWEEN`), `IN`, `IS NULL` and sorting, but not containment or overlap. `jsonb @>`, array containment and `tsvector @@` need a GIN index, which maps each element to the rows that contain it; range overlap `&&` and nearest-neighbour search need GiST. BRIN stores one summary per block range, so on 200,000 rows inserted in time order it takes 24 kB.
rules.avoid:
CREATE INDEX products_attrs_idx ON products (attrs);
-- B-tree on jsonb: unusable for attrs @> '{"color": "red"}'
rules.unless: BRIN only works while physical row order follows the column (append-only data with no updates that move rows); GIN is slower to update than a B-tree.

rules.rule: Keep transactions short and never wait on the network or a user inside one
rules.why: An open transaction keeps its row locks until it ends and, once it has a snapshot or a transaction ID, stops `VACUUM` from removing rows that died after it started, in every table. A call to a payment API inside `BEGIN … COMMIT` turns a slow third party into lock queues and table bloat.

rules.rule: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` for every application role
rules.why: A client that crashes or hangs after `BEGIN` leaves a session in state `idle in transaction` that keeps its locks, and its snapshot or transaction ID keeps holding back vacuum, with no time limit. The default is 0, meaning no limit. With a limit the server terminates such a session and rolls its transaction back.
rules.avoid: SHOW idle_in_transaction_session_timeout;  -- 0

rules.rule: Retry the whole transaction on SQLSTATE `40001` and `40P01`
rules.why: `40001` (serialization_failure) is how `REPEATABLE READ` and `SERIALIZABLE` report a conflict with a concurrent transaction, and `40P01` (deadlock_detected) is how the server breaks a lock cycle. Both mean "nothing was changed, run it again", and both are expected under load.
rules.avoid: -- treat every database error as fatal and show it to the user
rules.prefer:
-- pseudocode around each transaction
-- for attempt in 1..5:
--   BEGIN; ...statements...; COMMIT;  -> done
--   on SQLSTATE 40001 or 40P01: ROLLBACK, sleep with jitter, repeat
--   on any other error: ROLLBACK and raise
rules.unless: The retry must rerun the decision logic from the start, not only the last statement, and must not repeat side effects outside the database.

rules.rule: Choose the isolation level for each kind of transaction on purpose
rules.why: The default `READ COMMITTED` takes a new snapshot for every statement, so two queries in one transaction can see different data, and a check followed by a write can be invalidated in between. `REPEATABLE READ` gives one snapshot for the whole transaction; `SERIALIZABLE` also aborts transactions whose combined result could not occur in any serial order.
rules.unless: Above `READ COMMITTED` the application must retry on `40001`.

rules.rule: Lock rows in the same order in every transaction
rules.why: Two transactions that update rows 3 and 7 in opposite order each hold one row and wait for the other. After `deadlock_timeout` (1 s) the server detects the cycle and aborts one of them with `40P01`. Locking in one agreed order, such as ascending primary key, makes the cycle impossible.

rules.rule: Change a value with one `UPDATE` that computes it, not with a read followed by a write
rules.why: Under `READ COMMITTED` two sessions can both read a balance of 100, both subtract in application code and both write 90: one update is lost. A single `UPDATE … SET balance = balance - 10` locks the row and computes from its latest committed version.
rules.prefer:
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 10
WHERE id = $1 AND balance >= 10
RETURNING balance;
rules.unless: When the new value needs application logic, read the row with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` in the same transaction first.

rules.rule: Use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` instead of checking for a row and then inserting it
rules.why: Between the `SELECT` and the `INSERT` another session can insert the same key, so the code either fails with `23505` (unique_violation) or, without a unique constraint, creates a duplicate. `ON CONFLICT` decides atomically against a unique index.
rules.unless: It needs a unique index or constraint on the conflict columns, and `DO NOTHING` returns no row when the key already exists.

rules.rule: Claim queue rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
rules.why: With a plain `FOR UPDATE`, every worker asks for the same first row and waits behind the worker that holds it, so the queue runs one job at a time. `SKIP LOCKED` passes over rows that another transaction has locked, and each worker gets its own batch without waiting.
rules.avoid:
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued'
ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE;
rules.prefer:
WITH next AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued'
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 10
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE jobs j SET status = 'running', locked_at = now()
FROM next WHERE j.id = next.id
RETURNING j.id, j.payload;
rules.unless: Skipping rows gives an inconsistent view of the table, which is right for a queue and wrong for general queries.

rules.rule: Take advisory locks with `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, not the session-level form
rules.why: An advisory lock is an application-defined lock on a number. The session-level form stays held until `pg_advisory_unlock` or disconnect, even after rollback; behind a transaction-mode pooler the session belongs to the server connection, so the lock stays with whichever client gets that connection next. The transaction-level form is released at commit or rollback.

rules.rule: Never keep an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock open across other work
rules.why: `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, taken by `TRUNCATE`, `DROP`, `VACUUM FULL`, `LOCK TABLE` and most `ALTER TABLE` forms, conflicts with every other lock, including the one a `SELECT` takes. It is held until the transaction ends, so a slow statement after the DDL in the same transaction keeps the table unreadable.

rules.rule: Set `lock_timeout` before every DDL statement and retry when it expires
rules.why: DDL that needs `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` waits behind any running query on the table, and every new query on that table then queues behind the waiting DDL. One long report plus one `ALTER TABLE` stops all traffic to the table. With `lock_timeout` the DDL gives up with SQLSTATE `55P03` and the queue clears.
rules.avoid:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
-- waits without limit behind a long SELECT; everything else waits behind it

rules.rule: Add `CHECK` and foreign-key constraints as `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE` them separately
rules.why: A plain `ADD CONSTRAINT` scans the whole table while holding a lock that blocks writes (`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` for `CHECK`, `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` on both tables for a foreign key). With `NOT VALID` the constraint applies to new and updated rows at once and no scan happens; `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` then checks the old rows under `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`, which allows reads and writes.
rules.avoid:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_customer_id_fkey
  FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id);

rules.rule: Add `NOT NULL` to an existing column as a `NOT VALID` constraint, then validate it
rules.why: `ALTER COLUMN … SET NOT NULL` scans the whole table under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` to prove there are no NULLs. PostgreSQL 18 accepts `NOT NULL … NOT VALID`: new NULLs are rejected immediately (SQLSTATE `23502`) and `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` checks the existing rows under `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`.
rules.avoid: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET NOT NULL;
rules.unless: Before PostgreSQL 18, add `CHECK (customer_id IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, validate it, then run `SET NOT NULL`, which skips its scan when a valid `CHECK` proves the column has no NULLs.

rules.rule: Know which `ADD COLUMN` forms are instant and which rewrite the table
rules.why: A column with no default, a constant default, or a default that is fixed for the statement such as `now()` is added in the catalog only: existing rows are not touched. A volatile default (`clock_timestamp()`, `gen_random_uuid()`, `uuidv7()`), a stored generated column or an identity column rewrites the whole table and its indexes under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`. A virtual generated column, the default kind in PostgreSQL 18, never rewrites.
rules.avoid:
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD COLUMN public_id uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7();  -- full rewrite
rules.prefer:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN currency text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR';  -- instant

ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN public_id uuid;                -- instant
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN public_id SET DEFAULT uuidv7();  -- new rows only
-- then backfill existing rows in batches

rules.rule: Create and drop indexes in migrations with `CONCURRENTLY`, outside a transaction block
rules.why: `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes for the whole build, and `DROP INDEX` takes `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` on the table. The `CONCURRENTLY` forms avoid both but fail with an error inside `BEGIN … COMMIT`, which is how most migration tools wrap each file by default.
rules.unless: `IF NOT EXISTS` also skips an `INVALID` index left by a failed build, so check `pg_index.indisvalid` before relying on it.

rules.rule: Add a `UNIQUE` constraint by building the index concurrently, then attaching it with `USING INDEX`
rules.why: `ADD CONSTRAINT … UNIQUE` builds its index while holding `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so the table is unreadable for the whole build. Building the unique index with `CONCURRENTLY` first and then attaching it turns the constraint step into a brief catalog change.
rules.avoid:
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT orders_external_ref_key UNIQUE (external_ref);
rules.unless: If the concurrent build fails on a duplicate, drop the `INVALID` index, remove the duplicates and start again.

rules.rule: Backfill and mass-update in batches of a few thousand rows, each in its own transaction
rules.why: One `UPDATE` over a whole table holds every row lock until it commits, writes a new version of every row at once (doubling the table until vacuum catches up), produces a burst of WAL that replicas must replay, and keeps the vacuum horizon back while it runs. Small batches commit quickly and let vacuum and replication keep pace.
rules.avoid:
UPDATE orders SET external_ref = 'ord-' || id
WHERE external_ref IS NULL;  -- 200 million rows, one transaction
rules.prefer:
-- repeat until no row is left to update (a batch skips rows that other
-- sessions have locked); pause when replication lag grows
WITH batch AS (
  SELECT id FROM orders WHERE external_ref IS NULL
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE orders o SET external_ref = 'ord-' || o.id
FROM batch WHERE o.id = batch.id;

rules.rule: Rename columns and change types in expand-and-contract steps, not in place
rules.why: During a rolling deploy old and new application versions run together, so a rename breaks whichever version does not know the new name. Most type changes, such as `integer` to `bigint`, rewrite the table and its indexes under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`. Adding the new column, writing both, backfilling, switching reads and dropping the old column needs only brief locks and can be undone at each step.
rules.avoid:
ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN total TO total_amount;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN legacy_ref TYPE bigint;  -- full rewrite
rules.prefer:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN legacy_ref_big bigint;      -- 1. expand
-- 2. deploy code that writes both columns
-- 3. backfill legacy_ref_big in batches
-- 4. deploy code that reads and writes only the new column
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_ref;                 -- 5. contract
rules.unless: Widening `varchar(n)` or changing `varchar` to `text` does not rewrite the table and can be done in place.

rules.rule: Put a connection pooler between the application and PostgreSQL
rules.why: The server forks one operating-system process per connection, and opening one costs a fork, authentication and cache warm-up. A fleet of 40 application instances with 20 connections each asks for 800 backends, most of them idle. A pooler such as PgBouncer lets many client connections share a small number of server connections.
rules.avoid:
# every app instance connects directly
DATABASE_URL=postgres://orders_api@db-primary:5432/shop   # x 40 pods x 20
rules.prefer:
; pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
shop = host=db-primary port=5432 dbname=shop
[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 20
max_client_conn = 2000

rules.rule: Keep `max_connections` small and size pools from what the server can run at once
rules.why: The default is 100, and changing it needs a restart because it sizes shared memory. Each active backend can use `work_mem` several times over, so the worst-case memory grows with the connection count, and queries beyond what the CPUs and disks can run at once only wait inside the server while holding memory and locks. Waiting in the pooler queue is cheaper.
rules.avoid: max_connections = 2000   # "so the application never sees an error"
rules.prefer:
max_connections = 200            # postgresql.conf
superuser_reserved_connections = 3

; pooler: total server connections stay well below max_connections
default_pool_size = 20
rules.unless: Leave headroom for replication, backups, monitoring and an administrator session.

rules.rule: Under transaction-mode pooling, keep all session state inside the transaction
rules.why: In transaction mode a server connection is lent for one transaction and then given to another client. Anything set on the session stays behind on that server connection: `SET`, session advisory locks, temporary tables, SQL-level `PREPARE` and `LISTEN`. The next client inherits it, for example another tenant's `search_path`.
rules.unless: Protocol-level prepared statements work in transaction mode when the pooler tracks them (PgBouncer 1.21+ with `max_prepared_statements`); `LISTEN` and session temporary tables need a session-mode pool or a direct connection.

rules.rule: Set `statement_timeout` and related limits per role, not server-wide
rules.why: `statement_timeout`, `lock_timeout`, `transaction_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` all default to 0, meaning no limit, so one runaway query can hold a connection and its locks for hours. A server-wide value applies to every session, so it would also cancel migrations, index builds and manual maintenance; attach the limits to the roles that serve requests.
rules.avoid:
# postgresql.conf: also hits migrations, index builds and manual VACUUM
statement_timeout = '5s'
rules.unless: Role settings are applied when a session starts; a pooler that connects as one shared user needs the limits on that user, or `SET LOCAL` per transaction.

rules.rule: Give each service its own role and set `application_name` on every connection
rules.why: When every client connects as the same user with an empty `application_name`, `pg_stat_activity`, the logs and `pg_stat_statements` cannot tell which service holds a lock or sends a slow query. Separate roles also allow separate privileges, timeouts and connection limits.
rules.avoid: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/shop   # used by every service

rules.rule: Never turn autovacuum off, globally or per table
rules.why: Updates and deletes leave dead row versions that only `VACUUM` removes. Without it tables and indexes grow without bound, the visibility map goes stale so index-only scans read the heap, and planner statistics age. Even with `autovacuum = off` the server still forces vacuums to prevent transaction ID wraparound, at the worst possible time.
rules.avoid:
ALTER TABLE events SET (autovacuum_enabled = false);
-- or autovacuum = off in postgresql.conf
rules.unless: If autovacuum disturbs the workload, make it run more often with less work per run instead of stopping it.

rules.rule: Lower the autovacuum scale factors on large tables
rules.why: Autovacuum starts when dead rows exceed `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold` (50) plus `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` (0.2) times the row count. On a table of 100 million rows that is 20 million dead rows before the first vacuum. PostgreSQL 18 adds `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold`, which caps the result at 100,000,000 rows by default, but that is still far too late for most tables.
rules.avoid:
-- defaults on a 100-million-row table:
-- vacuum after 50 + 0.2 * 100,000,000 = 20,000,050 dead rows

rules.rule: Find and remove whatever holds back the vacuum horizon
rules.why: `VACUUM` can only remove rows that no transaction might still need. The oldest such point (the xmin horizon) is held back by four things: a long-running or idle-in-transaction session, an abandoned replication slot, a forgotten prepared transaction, and a standby with `hot_standby_feedback = on` running a long query. While one of them is old, vacuum runs but removes nothing, in every table.
rules.avoid:
-- VACUUM VERBOSE keeps reporting dead rows as "not yet removable"
-- and the response is to run VACUUM more often

rules.rule: Monitor transaction ID age and alert long before the limit
rules.why: Transaction IDs are 32-bit, so rows must be frozen before they are about 2 billion transactions old. At an age of `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` (200 million) autovacuum forces a freezing vacuum of the table. If freezing is blocked, the server warns when 40 million IDs remain and refuses to assign new transaction IDs when 3 million remain: all writes stop.
rules.avoid:
-- no alert on age(datfrozenxid); the first sign is
-- WARNING: database "shop" must be vacuumed within 39999999 transactions
rules.unless: An age that keeps rising past 200 million means freezing is blocked: look for what holds the xmin horizon before it reaches `vacuum_failsafe_age` (1.6 billion).

rules.rule: Lower `fillfactor` on tables that are updated often, and do not index the columns that change
rules.why: A HOT (heap-only tuple) update writes no index entries and its dead versions can be cleaned up without `VACUUM`. It is possible only when no column used by an index changes (BRIN indexes do not count) and the page has room for the new version. The default `fillfactor` of 100 packs pages full on insert, so an update of a row in a full page has to put the new version on another page and add an entry to every index.
rules.avoid:
CREATE INDEX sessions_last_seen_idx ON sessions (last_seen_at);
-- every "touch" of a session now writes the index too
rules.unless: A lower `fillfactor` makes the table larger, which slows scans; leave insert-only tables at 100.

rules.rule: Do not run `VACUUM FULL` on a live table; shrink it online instead
rules.why: `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table into a new file under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so nothing can read or write it until it finishes, and it needs free disk space for the complete new copy. Plain `VACUUM` already makes dead space reusable for new rows; a rewrite is needed only to give space back to the operating system.
rules.avoid: VACUUM FULL orders;   -- table offline for the duration
rules.prefer:
VACUUM (VERBOSE) orders;                  -- space becomes reusable
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_pkey;   -- rebuild a bloated index online
-- to shrink the table itself online: pg_repack, or copy into a
-- new table in batches and swap it in
rules.unless: In a maintenance window with enough disk space, `VACUUM FULL` is the simplest way to compact a table.

rules.rule: Delete old data by dropping partitions, or in small batches, never with one huge `DELETE`
rules.why: A `DELETE` of millions of rows writes WAL for each one and leaves each as a dead row that vacuum must find later; the file does not shrink. Dropping a partition removes its files at once and leaves nothing to vacuum. Data with a retention period should be partitioned by time from the start.
rules.avoid: DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days';
rules.unless: `DETACH … CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside a transaction block.

rules.rule: Run `pg_stat_statements` on every production server
rules.why: It records calls, total and mean time, rows and buffer usage per normalized statement, which shows what the server spends its time on. Without it the only evidence is individual slow-query log lines, which miss a fast query that runs a million times a day. It must be in `shared_preload_libraries`, so enabling it later needs a restart.
rules.avoid: shared_preload_libraries = ''   # nothing to look at during an incident

rules.rule: Read the plan with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` before changing a slow query
rules.why: The plan shows where the time goes: a sequential scan that filters out most rows, a sort that spills to disk, or a row estimate that is wrong by orders of magnitude. `BUFFERS` adds how many pages each node read, which does not vary with load the way timings do. PostgreSQL 18 includes buffer counts in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` automatically.
rules.avoid:
-- add an index because the query "looks like it needs one"
EXPLAIN SELECT ...;   -- estimates only, nothing measured

rules.rule: Log slow statements with `log_min_duration_statement` and their plans with `auto_explain`
rules.why: Neither is active by default (`log_min_duration_statement` is `-1` and `auto_explain` is not loaded), so a query that was slow at 03:00 leaves no trace. `log_min_duration_statement` logs the text and duration of statements over the threshold; `auto_explain` logs the plan that was actually used, which often differs from the plan obtained later with different parameters or statistics.
rules.avoid: log_min_duration_statement = -1   # default: nothing is logged
rules.prefer:
log_min_duration_statement = '500ms'
session_preload_libraries = 'auto_explain'
auto_explain.log_min_duration = '2s'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on
auto_explain.log_timing = off     # row counts without per-node clock reads
auto_explain.log_buffers = on
rules.unless: `auto_explain.log_analyze` instruments every statement, not only the slow ones; keep `log_timing` off or lower `auto_explain.sample_rate` on a busy server.

rules.rule: Turn on `track_io_timing` and `log_lock_waits`
rules.why: Both are off by default. `track_io_timing` adds read and write times to `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, `pg_stat_statements`, `pg_stat_io` and `pg_stat_database`, which separates "slow because of disk" from "slow because of CPU". `log_lock_waits` writes a log line whenever a session waits longer than `deadlock_timeout` (1 s) for a lock, naming the blocker.
rules.avoid:
track_io_timing = off
log_lock_waits = off
rules.prefer:
track_io_timing = on
log_lock_waits = on
deadlock_timeout = '1s'
rules.unless: On hardware with a slow clock source `track_io_timing` adds overhead; measure it with `pg_test_timing` first.

rules.rule: Size `work_mem` per sort or hash node, not per connection
rules.why: `work_mem` (default 4MB) is the limit for each sort or hash operation, in each backend and each parallel worker; hash operations may use `hash_mem_multiplier` (2.0) times as much. A query with four such nodes on 200 connections can ask for hundreds of times the setting, so a large global value ends in the out-of-memory killer. Too small a value makes sorts spill to temporary files.
rules.avoid: work_mem = '1GB'   # server-wide, with max_connections = 300

rules.rule: Set `shared_buffers` and `effective_cache_size` for the machine
rules.why: The default `shared_buffers` of 128MB suits a laptop. On a dedicated server with at least 1GB of RAM a reasonable start is 25% of RAM, and more than 40% rarely helps because PostgreSQL also relies on the operating-system cache. `effective_cache_size` (default 4GB) allocates nothing: it tells the planner how much data is probably cached, and a value that is too low makes it avoid index scans.
rules.avoid:
shared_buffers = 128MB          # default, on a 64GB server
effective_cache_size = 4GB      # default
rules.prefer:
# dedicated server with 64GB of RAM
shared_buffers = 16GB
effective_cache_size = 48GB     # shared_buffers + expected OS cache
rules.unless: Changing `shared_buffers` needs a restart, and a larger value usually calls for a larger `max_wal_size`.

rules.rule: Raise `max_wal_size` until checkpoints are started by the timer, not by WAL volume
rules.why: `max_wal_size` defaults to 1GB and `checkpoint_timeout` to 5 minutes. A write-heavy server reaches the WAL limit long before the timer and starts a checkpoint early. The first change to each page after a checkpoint writes the whole page to WAL, so frequent checkpoints multiply WAL volume, I/O and replication traffic.
rules.avoid:
max_wal_size = 1GB   # default, on a server that writes 1GB of WAL per minute
-- LOG: checkpoints are occurring too frequently (12 seconds apart)
rules.prefer:
max_wal_size = '16GB'          # sized so that the limit is rarely reached
checkpoint_timeout = '15min'

SELECT num_timed, num_requested FROM pg_stat_checkpointer;
-- healthy: num_timed grows, num_requested stays almost flat
rules.unless: A larger `max_wal_size` uses more disk in `pg_wal`, and a longer checkpoint interval means more WAL to replay after a crash.

rules.rule: Lower `random_page_cost` on SSD storage
rules.why: The planner prices a random page read at 4.0 and a sequential one at 1.0 by default, a ratio chosen for spinning disks. On flash storage random reads cost about the same as sequential ones, so with the default the planner chooses sequential scans and bitmap scans where an index scan would be faster.
rules.avoid: random_page_cost = 4.0   # default, on NVMe storage
rules.unless: Keep a higher value for network or spinning storage where random reads really are slower.

rules.rule: Keep planner statistics current, and add extended statistics for columns that depend on each other
rules.why: The planner chooses plans from row-count estimates built by `ANALYZE`. After a bulk load, or on a partitioned parent table (which autovacuum never analyzes), the statistics are missing or stale. For conditions on related columns such as `city` and `postal_code` the planner multiplies the two selectivities as if they were independent and underestimates the row count, often choosing a nested loop that runs far too many times.
rules.avoid: COPY measurements FROM STDIN;   -- then query at once, with no ANALYZE

rules.rule: Restore backups on a schedule; a backup that was never restored does not count
rules.why: A backup job can report success for months while producing something that cannot be restored: a missing WAL segment, an archive that silently stopped, a wrong retention setting. Only a restore into a scratch server, followed by a query against the data, proves the backup and shows how long recovery really takes.
rules.avoid:
# nightly cron; the exit code is the only check
pg_basebackup -D /backups/base/latest
rules.prefer:
# weekly, automated: verify, restore, start, query
pg_verifybackup /backups/base/latest
cp -a /backups/base/latest /restore/data
pg_ctl -D /restore/data -o "-p 5499" start
psql -p 5499 -d shop -c "SELECT max(created_at) FROM orders"
rules.unless: `pg_verifybackup` checks files against the backup manifest only; it does not replace starting a server from the backup. For a tar-format backup add `--no-parse-wal`, because it can check WAL only in plain format.

rules.rule: Take physical base backups and archive WAL continuously, so you can recover to any point in time
rules.why: A `pg_dump` is a snapshot of one moment: everything written after it is lost, and restoring a large database from SQL takes hours. A base backup plus the archived WAL since then can be replayed to any moment (point-in-time recovery), for example to one second before a mistaken `DELETE`. A replica is not a backup, because the `DELETE` is replicated too.
rules.avoid:
# the only backup
pg_dump shop > /backups/shop.sql   # nightly
rules.prefer:
# postgresql.conf (or let pgBackRest / Barman manage it)
wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=shop archive-push %p'

# recovery: restore the base backup, then
restore_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=shop archive-get %f "%p"'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-15 09:41:00+00'
rules.unless: Keep `pg_dump` for moving single tables or upgrading across major versions; it complements physical backups.

rules.rule: Alert when WAL archiving fails or falls behind
rules.why: When `archive_command` keeps failing, the server retries the same segment and keeps every unarchived segment in `pg_wal`. The directory grows until the file system is full and the server shuts down with a PANIC, and point-in-time recovery cannot go past the last archived segment. `pg_stat_archiver` shows the failures long before that.
rules.avoid:
-- archive_command set once and never checked;
-- the first sign of a broken archive is a full disk on the primary
rules.unless: `pg_ls_archive_statusdir()` needs a superuser or a member of `pg_monitor`.

rules.rule: Monitor replication lag both in bytes and in time
rules.why: Lag in bytes on the primary shows how much WAL a standby still has to receive or replay, which is the data at risk in a failover. Lag in time on the standby shows how stale its reads are. Each hides a case: on an idle primary the time since the last replayed transaction keeps growing although nothing is missing, and a byte count says little about how old the data is.
rules.avoid:
-- only checks that a standby is connected
SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_replication;
rules.prefer:
-- on the primary
SELECT application_name, state, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn) AS replay_lag_bytes,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- on the standby
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay;

rules.rule: Limit and monitor every replication slot
rules.why: A replication slot makes the primary keep all WAL its consumer has not confirmed. `max_slot_wal_keep_size` defaults to `-1` (unlimited), so a standby or logical subscriber that went away fills the disk of the primary until it stops accepting writes. With a limit, the slot is invalidated instead and only that consumer has to be rebuilt.
rules.avoid: max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1   # default: a dead slot retains WAL forever
rules.prefer:
max_slot_wal_keep_size = '50GB'
idle_replication_slot_timeout = '2d'   # PostgreSQL 18

SELECT slot_name, active, wal_status, safe_wal_size, inactive_since,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots;
rules.unless: Size the limit above the longest outage a consumer should survive; an invalidated slot cannot be resumed.

rules.rule: Decide per workload whether a commit must reach a standby before it is acknowledged
rules.why: With asynchronous replication, the default, a failover loses the commits that the standby had not received. Naming standbys in `synchronous_standby_names` makes each commit wait until a standby has flushed it, which costs a network round trip per commit, and commits wait without limit when no synchronous standby is available. `synchronous_commit` can be relaxed per transaction for data that can be lost.
rules.avoid: synchronous_standby_names = 'pg2'   # one named standby: its outage stops all commits
rules.unless: `synchronous_commit = off` can lose the last transactions in a crash (up to three times `wal_writer_delay`) but never corrupts data.

rules.rule: Run failover through an HA manager with a consensus store and fencing, not a hand-written script
rules.why: A script that promotes a standby when the primary stops answering cannot tell a dead primary from a network partition. If the old primary is still running, two servers accept writes (split brain) and one side of the data is lost. A manager such as Patroni holds a leader lease in a consensus store (etcd), and promotes a standby only after that lease has expired. A primary that cannot renew its lease demotes itself before then (self-fencing), so two servers never accept writes at once.
rules.avoid:
# cron on the standby
pg_isready -h pg1 || pg_ctl promote -D /var/lib/postgresql/data
rules.prefer:
# patroni.yml (excerpt)
bootstrap:
  dcs:
    ttl: 30
    loop_wait: 10
    retry_timeout: 10
    maximum_lag_on_failover: 1048576
postgresql:
  use_pg_rewind: true

rules.rule: Rehearse a planned switchover regularly
rules.why: A failover path that has never been exercised fails in new ways during an outage: clients that keep the old address, a standby with different settings, sequences or extensions missing on the other side. A planned switchover in a quiet hour tests routing, client reconnection and the rejoin of the old primary while both servers are healthy.
rules.avoid: -- the first role change of the cluster happens during an incident
rules.unless: Applications must reconnect and retry: every connection to the old primary is closed.

rules.rule: Run with data checksums enabled
rules.why: Without checksums a page damaged by storage or memory is read as valid data and spreads into backups and replicas unnoticed. With checksums the server verifies each page it reads from disk and reports the failure. `initdb` enables them by default since PostgreSQL 18; a cluster created earlier keeps its old setting.
rules.avoid: initdb --no-data-checksums -D /var/lib/postgresql/data
rules.prefer:
SHOW data_checksums;   -- on

SELECT datname, checksum_failures, checksum_last_failure
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE checksum_failures > 0;

# enable on an existing cluster, with the server cleanly shut down
pg_checksums --enable -D /var/lib/postgresql/data
rules.unless: `pg_checksums --enable` rewrites every data file while the server is down, so plan it per node behind a switchover.

rules.rule: Never connect an application as a superuser or as the owner of its tables
rules.why: A superuser bypasses every permission check and row-level security, can read server files and run programs through `COPY`, so one SQL injection becomes control of the server. A table owner can drop or alter the table and is exempt from its row-level security policies. The application needs neither.
rules.avoid: DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:secret@db:5432/shop
rules.prefer:
CREATE ROLE app_owner NOLOGIN;            -- owns the schema, runs migrations
CREATE ROLE orders_api LOGIN;              -- what the service connects as

SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolbypassrls
FROM pg_roles WHERE rolcanlogin AND (rolsuper OR rolbypassrls);

rules.rule: Grant each role only the privileges it uses, and set default privileges for future tables
rules.why: A role that can only `SELECT` cannot be used to delete data, whatever bug the service has. Grants apply to existing objects only: a table created by the next migration has no grants, so the service fails with `42501` (insufficient_privilege) unless `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` was set for the role that creates tables.
rules.avoid:
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app TO orders_api;
GRANT ALL ON DATABASE shop TO PUBLIC;
rules.unless: Default privileges cover only objects created later by the named role; grant on existing tables separately.

rules.rule: Authenticate with `scram-sha-256`, and order `pg_hba.conf` from specific to general
rules.why: The server uses the first `pg_hba.conf` line that matches the connection type, address, database and user, and never falls through to a later one: a broad `trust` or `md5` line above a strict line makes the strict one dead. `trust` asks for no password at all, and MD5 password support is deprecated in PostgreSQL 18. `password_encryption` already defaults to `scram-sha-256`.
rules.avoid:
# TYPE  DATABASE  USER        ADDRESS       METHOD
host    all       all         0.0.0.0/0     trust
hostssl shop      orders_api  10.0.1.0/24   scram-sha-256   # never reached
rules.prefer:
# TYPE  DATABASE  USER        ADDRESS       METHOD
hostssl shop      orders_api  10.0.1.0/24   scram-sha-256
hostssl shop      reporting   10.0.2.0/24   scram-sha-256
host    all       all         all           reject
rules.unless: Roles whose password is still stored as an MD5 hash must set it again before they can use SCRAM.

rules.rule: Connect with TLS and `sslmode=verify-full`
rules.why: The client default `sslmode=prefer` encrypts only if the server offers it and never checks who the server is, and `require` encrypts without checking either. Anyone who can redirect the connection can then pose as the server and read or change everything sent over it. `verify-full` checks the certificate chain against a trusted root and that the host name matches the certificate.
rules.avoid: postgres://orders_api@db.internal:5432/shop?sslmode=require
rules.prefer:
postgres://orders_api@db.internal:5432/shop?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/db-ca.pem

# postgresql.conf
ssl = on
# pg_hba.conf: hostssl lines only, so unencrypted connections are refused

rules.rule: Enforce tenant isolation with row-level security, not only with a `WHERE` clause in the application
rules.why: If isolation depends on every query including `tenant_id = …`, one forgotten filter shows one tenant the data of another. A row-level security policy adds the condition to every statement on the table. Table owners, superusers and `BYPASSRLS` roles skip policies, so the application must connect as none of these, or the table must use `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.
rules.avoid:
-- isolation by convention
SELECT id, title FROM documents WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = $2;
rules.unless: Policies run for every row considered, so index `tenant_id` and keep policy expressions simple.

rules.rule: Set `search_path` on every `SECURITY DEFINER` function, with `pg_temp` last
rules.why: A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with the privileges of its owner but resolves unqualified names through the caller's `search_path`. A caller can put a schema of their own first in that path, and the temporary schema is searched first for tables and types unless the path names `pg_temp`, so a caller can create an object with the same name and have the function use it with the owner's rights. Functions are also executable by `PUBLIC` when created.

rules.rule: Make sure ordinary roles cannot create objects in the `public` schema
rules.why: `public` is on the default `search_path` of every role. A role that can create objects there can define a function or operator that another user then calls by its unqualified name, running the attacker's code with that user's privileges. New databases since PostgreSQL 15 allow only the database owner to create in `public`, but a database upgraded from version 14 or earlier keeps the old grant to everyone.
rules.avoid:
-- upgraded database: nspacl of public still contains "=UC/postgres"
SELECT nspacl FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname = 'public';

rules.rule: Keep passwords and secrets out of SQL text and server logs
rules.why: A statement is logged with its full text when it is slow, fails, or matches `log_statement`. `ALTER ROLE … PASSWORD '…'` therefore puts the password in the server log and in the client history, and a secret written as a literal ends up in every log shipper. Bind parameter values are logged with slow statements too, because `log_parameter_max_length` defaults to `-1` (full).
rules.avoid:
ALTER ROLE orders_api PASSWORD 'S3cret!';
SELECT pgp_sym_encrypt(card_number, 'hard-coded-key') FROM cards;
rules.unless: Setting `log_parameter_max_length = 0` also removes parameter values that help when debugging slow statements.

rules.rule: Tune queries and use a larger server before you distribute the data
rules.why: One PostgreSQL server keeps every transaction, join and constraint local and correct. Splitting data across nodes turns joins into network calls, makes cross-node transactions need two-phase commit, and multiplies operations work. Most load problems come from a few statements that a missing index, a pooler or more memory fix at a fraction of that cost.
rules.avoid:
-- "the database is slow, so we need sharding"
-- no pg_stat_statements, no EXPLAIN, default configuration

rules.rule: Send reads to replicas only where stale data is acceptable
rules.why: A streaming replica replays WAL after the primary has committed, so it is always somewhat behind. A user who saves a form and is then served from a replica may not see the change. Even a synchronous standby with the default `synchronous_commit = on` has only flushed the WAL, not applied it; only `remote_apply` waits until the change is visible there.
rules.avoid:
-- write on the primary, then read the same row from a replica
INSERT INTO comments (post_id, body) VALUES ($1, $2);   -- primary
SELECT id, body FROM comments WHERE post_id = $1;        -- replica: may miss it
rules.unless: `remote_apply` only covers standbys listed in `synchronous_standby_names` and adds their replay time to every such commit.

rules.rule: Partition a table only when queries filter on the partition key or old data is dropped in bulk
rules.why: Partitioning pays off in two cases: the planner can skip partitions because the query constrains the key (pruning), and a whole partition can be dropped instead of deleting rows. Otherwise it only adds cost: every query without the key visits every partition, primary keys and unique constraints must include the partition key, and thousands of partitions slow planning. It is usually worthwhile only once a table is larger than memory.
rules.unless: Create future partitions ahead of time (or a `DEFAULT` partition), because an insert with no matching partition fails.

rules.rule: Load large amounts of data with `COPY`, not with single-row `INSERT` statements
rules.why: Each single-row `INSERT` in its own transaction pays a round trip, a parse and a WAL flush at commit. `COPY` sends all rows in one command and one transaction and is almost always faster than `INSERT`, even batched inserts with prepared statements. Build secondary indexes after the load and run `ANALYZE` when it is done.
rules.unless: `COPY` fails on the first bad row (`ON_ERROR ignore` skips only rows whose values cannot be converted to the column type, not constraint violations), and it cannot upsert: load into a staging table and `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` from there.

rules.rule: Precompute expensive aggregates that are read often, and refresh them without blocking readers
rules.why: A dashboard that aggregates millions of rows on every page view spends the same CPU and I/O again for an answer that changes slowly. A materialized view stores the result as a table. A plain `REFRESH` locks out readers while it runs; `REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY` keeps the old contents readable and needs a unique index on the view.
rules.unless: A materialized view is as stale as its last refresh and each refresh recomputes the whole query; for large data keep an incrementally updated summary table instead.

rules.rule: Write events for other systems to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data change
rules.why: Publishing to a message broker and committing to the database are two separate operations: if the process dies between them, either the event is sent for a change that rolled back or the change commits and the event is lost. An outbox row commits or rolls back with the change, and a separate worker delivers it afterwards with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
rules.unless: Delivery is at least once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates; delete or drop delivered rows regularly so the table stays small.

rules.rule: Shard only when a measured limit of one primary remains after everything else
rules.why: Sharding (splitting rows across independent servers by a key) is the one step that scales writes, and the hardest to undo. Queries without the shard key fan out to every node, transactions across shards need two-phase commit, and a poorly chosen key cannot be changed without moving the data. It is justified when write volume or data size exceeds one server after tuning, replicas, partitioning and archiving.
